prime.problem: When an agent run goes wrong, one word usually hides the answer. "Done", "tool", "session" and "memory" each cover two jobs owned by two parts of the system, so a check on one job gets read as a check on the other, and every failure gets filed as "the agent was weird".
prime.fits: Second card of the map. The ten-layers card sorted the stack by what each layer owns; this card shows the seams between those owners, using the claim chain from the Tuesday run that the rest of the series keeps returning to.
expect: nine boundary pairs (session ≠ authorization … profile ≠ sandbox)
layer collapse as an architecture error, not a naming error
prime.goal: Take any overloaded word in an agent system, name the two owners it hides, and predict the concrete failure you get if one record serves both.

attend: In the Tuesday run, which two meanings of "done" are true and which owner certifies each one?
Why does the step-7 compaction summary make the step-9 reply wrong, even though no tool lied?
Why does an approval gate not stop a shell command that never calls the approval?
In the Hermes canary test, why is the comparison between the two Docker runs cleaner than local vs Docker?
What goes wrong when traces and audit records share one log bucket, for each of their two audiences?

must: One word covers two jobs → each job has a different owner and a different failure → a check on one is read as a check on the other → the failure is blamed on the wrong layer ("the agent was weird")

"Done" spans run, tools, command and task → the runtime can truthfully report the first two while the command exited 1 → a reply that says "done" claims all four → only a separate verifier receipt can confirm the task

Transcript ≠ context → compaction rewrites history into a summary the model reads instead of the raw tool output → "1 failed" can become "tests passing" → the false claim starts from the summary, not from the model inventing it

Approval decides whether, isolation decides how far → an approval only guards the paths that call it → a blocked command proves nothing about the shell or the mounts → containment has to come from the OS, container mounts or service credentials
elevated: Hermes Part 5's posture is the effective mount table, not the label "runs in Docker" → the container still had /workspace read-write plus eleven read-only mounts → adding one read-only mount restored read access to the sibling file → audit the real mounts, user and network, not the configuration story
reference: the exact post titles and section names
Hermes version v0.21.0 and the 4 September 2026 run date

compress.prompt: Card closed: write the four meanings of "done" with the owner of each, mark which were true in the Tuesday run, then pick three of the nine pairs and for each write one sentence on what breaks when they are merged.
checklist: run done (control plane) ✓, tools done (runtime) ✓, command done (execution surface) ✗ exit 1, task done (verifier) ✗
the reply's "done" claims all four; the compaction summary upgraded "1 failed" to "tests passing"
each pair names two owners, not two synonyms
a failure per pair from the posts, e.g. shared room shared authority, guardrail mistaken for containment, label with no owner
the diagnostic question is which owner failed, not whether the agent was smart

retrieve.q: Explain the difference between a session and authorization using a shared team chat with one tool-enabled agent, and say what per-user sessions do and don't protect.
answer: session: which interaction owns the turn, and its state and memory
authorization: who may read, change or act
per-user sessions separate state and privacy, but everyone in the room still steers the same tools
OpenClaw 5: shared room, shared authority

retrieve.q: Walk the Tuesday run from step 6 to the checker and say, at each step, which owner's record changed and what it said.
answer: step 6: execution surface records pytest exit 1, 1 failed / 41 passed; runtime records the tool call as completed
step 7: compaction writes a summary claiming tests pass; the model's context now holds the summary, not the raw output
step 9: the model writes "Done … all tests pass" and the control plane delivers it
checker: an independent pytest run exits 1, so the task is not verified

retrieve.q: In the Hermes canary experiment, list the three postures and the result of each, and say which pair of runs isolates a single variable.
answer: local backend: sibling file readable (inherits the host user's authority)
Docker, sibling not mounted: FileNotFoundError
Docker, sibling mounted read-only: readable again
the two Docker runs differ by one mount; local vs Docker changes OS identity, namespace and backend at once

retrieve.q: Your team wants one log stream for everything the agent does. Argue for or against splitting traces from audit records, naming the cost of each choice.
answer: one stream is simpler and shares identifiers
but debug logs become too sensitive for broad engineering access
and the audit record becomes too weak for accountability
Part 8: share identifiers, not responsibilities; split once the agent changes the outside world

compare.q: The agent-loop card treats end_turn as "the model thinks it's finished, check if you can". This card splits "done" into four owners. What does the four-way split add, and which design choice in the loop causes the gap it fills?
answer: the loop only sees stop reasons, which belong to the model
the four-way split adds the execution and verifier records the loop doesn't own
the gap comes from the harness trusting model text as its completion signal
pick the simple check for throwaway runs, the split once someone must explain or trust the result

compare.q: This card lists approval ≠ isolation as one of nine pairs; the approval-not-isolation card tests it with a toy harness and the Hermes canary. What does that test add that naming the pair can't, and would either control have stopped the Tuesday run's false "done"?
answer: naming the pair says two owners exist; the test shows a control is only as wide as its path: the approved write_file was blocked while a shell write to the same folder exited 0
the canary shows reach is set by the backend and its mounts, not by the profile: FileNotFoundError without the mount, readable with one read-only mount
neither control stops a false claim: the Tuesday "done" is words, so it needs the third receipt, verification
an approval whose evidence line quoted the step-7 summary would even approve pushing a still-failing test

predict.q: Suppose the harness never compacts: the model sees the raw 1 failed, 41 passed output at step 9. Does the false success claim disappear, and which of the four "done" rows would still be able to disagree with the reply?
predict.answer: Not necessarily. Removing compaction removes one cause (the summary that upgraded the status), but the model's reply is still unverified text, and models can misread or overstate long tool output. The command and task rows can still be ✗ while the reply says done; only the verifier's independent re-run settles it. The split matters even when every record is accurate, because the reply is a claim, not a receipt.

apply.task: Take one real run of your own agent (a mini-swe-agent or Claude Code transcript). Find every place a word like "done", "fixed", "passing" or "saved" appears in the model's text. For each one, write which of the four rows (run, tools, command, task) it claims, and point to the record in the transcript that would confirm it, or write "no receipt".
apply.done: A table with one row per claim word, its row type, and either a pointer to a tool output or exit code, or "no receipt"; plus a count of claims that had no receipt.
apply.hint: Exit codes and test counts usually sit in the tool result just before the claim. A claim made after a compaction or summary step is the first place to look for a missing receipt.
